title: Data types: what Fabric Warehouse stores and what it rejects
summary: Fabric Warehouse tables accept fewer column types than SQL Server. nvarchar, nchar, datetime, smalldatetime, datetimeoffset, money, smallmoney, tinyint, text, ntext, image, xml, sql_variant, geography and geometry cannot be table column types. datetime2 and time are limited to precision 6 in tables. Many of these types still appear at query time: GETDATE returns datetime, SYSDATETIME returns datetime2(7), SYSDATETIMEOFFSET returns datetimeoffset(7), and CAST to xml or geography compiles and returns xml or geography. Always CAST to a storable type before you persist a value. Use varchar with a UTF-8 collation instead of nvarchar, datetime2(6) instead of datetime, datetime2(7) or datetimeoffset, decimal(19,4) instead of money, smallint instead of tinyint, and varchar(max) for XML or well-known text. varchar(max), varbinary(max) and uniqueidentifier are usable. The expression probes below check result types. The CREATE TABLE probes are low confidence because a compile-only check may not validate column types.

claims.statement: nvarchar still works in expressions; only table columns reject it. To store Unicode text, CAST to varchar, which uses a UTF-8 collation in Fabric Warehouse.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT CAST(N'déjà vu' AS nvarchar(10)) AS c;
claims.sql_server: SQL Server allows nvarchar and nchar columns in tables.
claims.alternative: SELECT CAST(N'déjà vu' AS varchar(40)) AS c; -- size varchar in bytes: UTF-8 characters can take up to 4 bytes

claims.statement: A CREATE TABLE with an nvarchar or nchar column is rejected in Fabric Warehouse.
claims.sql_server: SQL Server accepts this CREATE TABLE.

claims.statement: GETDATE returns datetime, which a Fabric table column cannot use. Cast it to datetime2(6) before you insert it or select it into a table.
claims.alternative: SELECT CAST(GETDATE() AS datetime2(6)) AS c;

claims.statement: SYSDATETIME returns datetime2(7), but table columns allow at most datetime2(6). CAST to datetime2(6) before you persist the value.
claims.sql_server: SQL Server allows datetime2(7) columns. datetime2 without a precision defaults to 7.
claims.alternative: SELECT CAST(SYSDATETIME() AS datetime2(6)) AS c;

claims.statement: CAST to datetime2(6) gives the storable precision. Always write the precision explicitly: datetime2 without a precision means datetime2(7).
claims.probe_sql: SELECT CAST('2024-05-01T10:20:30.1234567' AS datetime2(6)) AS c;

claims.statement: A CREATE TABLE column declared as datetime2(7), or as plain datetime2, is rejected because table columns allow at most precision 6.
SYSDATETIMEOFFSET returns datetimeoffset(7), and datetimeoffset cannot be a table column type. Normalize the value to UTC with AT TIME ZONE, then CAST it to datetime2(6).
claims.probe_sql: SELECT CAST(SYSDATETIMEOFFSET() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS datetime2(6)) AS c;
claims.alternative: Store a UTC datetime2(6) column. If you need the original offset, store it in a separate smallint column.

claims.statement: money and smallmoney can appear in expressions but not in table columns. Use decimal(19,4) for money and decimal(10,4) for smallmoney.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT CAST(CAST(12.3456 AS money) AS decimal(19,4)) AS c;
claims.sql_server: SQL Server allows money and smallmoney columns.

claims.statement: tinyint cannot be a table column type. Use smallint. A CAST to tinyint in a query still yields tinyint, so cast to smallint before you persist.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT CAST(200 AS tinyint) AS c;
claims.alternative: SELECT CAST(200 AS smallint) AS c;

claims.statement: varchar(max) is the replacement for text, ntext and nvarchar(max) in a Warehouse. In the SQL analytics endpoint of a Lakehouse, long strings may be exposed as varchar(8000) and truncated.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT CAST('abc' AS varchar(max)) AS c;

claims.statement: uniqueidentifier is supported, and NEWID works. NEWSEQUENTIALID is not supported, so a column default of NEWSEQUENTIALID will fail.
claims.sql_server: SQL Server allows NEWSEQUENTIALID as a column default.
claims.alternative: Generate keys with NEWID at insert time.

claims.statement: sql_variant cannot be a column type, and SQL_VARIANT_PROPERTY is not supported, so code that inspects variant base types fails.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT SQL_VARIANT_PROPERTY(CAST(1 AS sql_variant), 'BaseType') AS c;
claims.sql_server: SQL Server supports sql_variant columns and SQL_VARIANT_PROPERTY.
claims.alternative: Store the value as varchar plus a separate type-tag column.

claims.statement: xml works in query expressions: a CAST to xml compiles and returns xml. xml cannot be a table column type, so CAST XML text to varchar(max) before you persist it.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT CAST('1' AS xml) AS c;
claims.sql_server: SQL Server supports the xml type and xml columns.
claims.alternative: SELECT CAST('1' AS varchar(max)) AS c;

claims.statement: geography works in query expressions: a CAST to geography compiles and returns geography. geography and geometry cannot be table column types, so store well-known text in varchar, or store coordinates as float columns.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT CAST('POINT(1 1)' AS geography) AS c;
claims.sql_server: SQL Server supports geography and geometry columns.
claims.alternative: Store WKT in varchar(max), or latitude and longitude as float.
